strumenti/uraniborg/luce: Visible light, with the naked eye
strumenti/uraniborg/cosa: The most accurate observatory before the telescope was invented. There were no lenses: the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe measured the positions of stars and planets with large metal quadrants and sextants, aimed by eye like a gunsight.
strumenti/uraniborg/dove: On the island of Hven, in the strait between Denmark and Sweden (today it is called Ven and belongs to Sweden). King Frederick II of Denmark gave it to him as a gift in 1576.
strumenti/uraniborg/quando: Tycho worked there from 1576 to 1597. Today only the foundations of the castle and a museum remain.
strumenti/uraniborg/scoperte: Measurements accurate to about one arcminute, a thirtieth of the Moon's diameter: ten times better than anyone before him. Tycho showed that the comet of 1577 was further away than the Moon, so the heavens were not unchanging after all. After his death Johannes Kepler used his measurements of Mars to discover that the planets travel along ellipses (Kepler's laws, 1609 and 1619).
strumenti/uraniborg/origine: Uraniborg means "castle of Urania", the Greek muse of astronomy. Next to it Tycho also built Stjerneborg, "castle of the stars", with its instruments half sunk into the ground to shelter them from the wind.
strumenti/uraniborg/curiosita: Tycho had lost the tip of his nose in a duel as a student and wore a metal replacement. In 1572 he had already observed a "new star" in Cassiopeia: today we know it was a supernova.
strumenti/galileo/cosa: A tube of wood and paper with two lenses, built by Galileo Galilei in Padua by copying and improving on a Dutch invention. It magnified about 20 times and had a narrow field of view: it showed less than half the Moon at a time.
strumenti/galileo/dove: The two original telescopes that have survived are in the Museo Galileo in Florence.
strumenti/galileo/quando: Galileo pointed it at the sky between the end of 1609 and the beginning of 1610. He described his discoveries in the Sidereus Nuncius ("Starry Messenger"), published in Venice in March 1610.
strumenti/galileo/scoperte: The mountains and craters of the Moon; the countless stars of the Milky Way; on 7 January 1610 the four largest moons of Jupiter; then the phases of Venus and sunspots. The phases of Venus were evidence that the planets go round the Sun.
strumenti/galileo/origine: Galileo called it "occhiale" (Italian for "eyeglass") or, in Latin, "perspicillum". The word "telescope" was coined in 1611 at a dinner in Rome in Galileo's honour, at the Accademia dei Lincei: it was proposed by the Greek mathematician Giovanni Demisiani, who joined two Greek words, tele (far) and skopein (to look).
strumenti/galileo/curiosita: Today a 50-euro pair of binoculars shows the sky better than Galileo's telescope: you can already see Jupiter's moons with a 10×50 held steady.
strumenti/newton/tipo: The first reflecting telescope (with a mirror)
strumenti/newton/cosa: A small telescope, about 15 cm long, that uses a curved mirror of polished metal, just over 3 cm wide, instead of a main lens. Isaac Newton built it with his own hands, mirror included.
strumenti/newton/dove: A historic copy is kept at the Royal Society in London, to which Newton presented it between 1671 and 1672.
strumenti/newton/scoperte: It wasn't used for new discoveries, but it solved a problem: the lenses of refracting telescopes create coloured fringes around objects (chromatic aberration), whereas a mirror does not. At a magnification of 40 Newton could clearly see Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus.
strumenti/newton/origine: Ever since then, the design with a main mirror and a small, flat, tilted mirror has been called "Newtonian".
strumenti/newton/curiosita: Almost all of today's large telescopes are reflectors, and the Newtonian is still one of the telescopes most often recommended to beginners (the Dobsonian, for example).
strumenti/herschel-40/cosa: A gigantic reflector with a tube 12 metres long (40 English feet) and a metal mirror 1.2 metres across, built by William Herschel, a musician who became an astronomer. For half a century it was the largest telescope in the world.
strumenti/herschel-40/dove: In Slough, near Windsor, in England. Today a section of its tube survives at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.
strumenti/herschel-40/quando: It came into use in 1789 and was dismantled in 1840.
strumenti/herschel-40/scoperte: In its first few weeks Herschel discovered two moons of Saturn, Enceladus and Mimas (1789). Earlier, on 13 March 1781, with a smaller telescope he had built himself in Bath, he had discovered Uranus, the first planet found with a telescope.
strumenti/herschel-40/origine: It is named after its size, "40 feet". Herschel wanted to call Uranus "Georgium Sidus", George's star, in honour of King George III, who paid his salary; in the end the mythological name proposed by the German Johann Bode won out.
strumenti/herschel-40/curiosita: He was helped by his sister Caroline, who discovered eight comets and was the first woman to be paid to work as an astronomer. In 1800 William also discovered infrared light, by placing a thermometer beyond the red end of the rainbow made by a prism.
strumenti/leviatano/cosa: A telescope with a metal mirror 1.83 metres across and a 16-metre tube, slung between two stone walls. It was built by William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse. It was the largest in the world from 1845 to 1917.
strumenti/leviatano/dove: In the grounds of Birr Castle, in Ireland. It was restored in the 1990s and can be visited.
strumenti/leviatano/scoperte: In April 1845 Lord Rosse was the first to see and draw the spiral shape of a "nebula", M51, now known as the Whirlpool Galaxy. Nobody yet knew these were distant galaxies, but his drawing went all round Europe.
strumenti/leviatano/origine: The Leviathan is the sea monster of the Bible, a nod to the telescope's enormous size. Parsonstown was the old name of the town of Birr.
strumenti/leviatano/curiosita: Ireland's skies are often cloudy: Lord Rosse only managed to observe well on a few nights a year.
strumenti/brera/cosa: A telescope with a lens almost 22 centimetres across (218 mm) and more than 3 metres long, built in Munich by the Merz company and used by Giovanni Virginio Schiaparelli at the Brera Observatory in Milan.
strumenti/brera/dove: The Brera Observatory, founded by the Jesuits in 1764 in the Palazzo di Brera, is now part of INAF, Italy's National Institute for Astrophysics. The telescope is on display in the Brera Astronomical Museum.
strumenti/brera/quando: Ordered in 1862, the year Schiaparelli became director, it arrived at Brera in 1865 and began regular observations in 1875, from the new dome on the roof of the palazzo.
strumenti/brera/scoperte: During the opposition of Mars in 1877 Schiaparelli drew the most detailed map of the planet ever made up to then, with seas and "canali". Many of the names of Martian regions we still use today are his.
strumenti/brera/origine: Brera comes from "braida", a Lombardic word for an open field within a town. Merz is the surname of Georg Merz, the German optician who built it.
strumenti/brera/curiosita: Schiaparelli's "canali" (Italian for "channels") were natural grooves: translated into English as "canals", meaning man-made waterways, they gave rise to the legend of the Martians. Schiaparelli also discovered that the Perseid meteor shower comes from the dust of a comet.
strumenti/hooker/nome: The Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson
strumenti/hooker/cosa: A reflector with a glass mirror 2.5 metres (100 inches) across, the largest in the world from 1917 to 1948.
strumenti/hooker/dove: On Mount Wilson, at 1,740 metres, above Los Angeles (California).
strumenti/hooker/quando: First light in November 1917. It still works today, mainly for research and public evenings.
strumenti/hooker/scoperte: In 1923 Edwin Hubble used it to spot a variable star inside the Andromeda "nebula" and worked out that it was extremely far away: Andromeda is another galaxy. In 1929 Hubble, with Milton Humason, showed that galaxies are moving away from each other: the universe is expanding.
strumenti/hooker/origine: It is named after John D. Hooker, a Los Angeles businessman who paid for the mirror. The mountain is named after Benjamin Davis Wilson, who in 1864 cut the first trail up it to look for timber.
strumenti/hooker/curiosita: The lights of Los Angeles, which has grown enormously, now make the sky above Mount Wilson very bright: this is light pollution.
strumenti/palomar/nome: The Hale Telescope at Palomar Mountain
strumenti/palomar/cosa: A reflector with a 5-metre (200-inch) mirror weighing 14 tonnes. It was the most powerful telescope in the world for about forty years.
strumenti/palomar/dove: On Palomar Mountain, at about 1,700 metres, in southern California.
strumenti/palomar/quando: Opened in 1948, it is still in use today.
strumenti/palomar/scoperte: In 1963 Maarten Schmidt realised that the "star" 3C 273 was actually extremely far away and enormously powerful: it was the first quasar to be recognised, the heart of a galaxy with a giant black hole. In 1993, with a smaller telescope at the same observatory, comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 was discovered; the following year it crashed into Jupiter.
strumenti/palomar/origine: Named after George Ellery Hale, the astronomer who raised the money but died in 1938, before seeing it finished. "Palomar" is Spanish for dovecote.
strumenti/palomar/curiosita: The mirror was cast in Pyrex glass in 1934 and crossed the United States by train, at low speed, followed by the newspapers like a celebrity.
strumenti/jansky/cosa: An antenna 30 metres long, mounted on car wheels so it could be turned round in a circle. The engineer Karl Jansky built it for Bell Telephone Laboratories to find out where the interference on radio telephone calls was coming from.
strumenti/jansky/dove: In Holmdel, New Jersey (United States). A replica stands at the Green Bank observatory.
strumenti/jansky/quando: The measurements ran from 1931 to 1932; the discovery was published in 1933.
strumenti/jansky/scoperte: As well as thunderstorms, Jansky found a faint hiss that came every day from one particular direction in the sky: the centre of our galaxy, towards the constellation of Sagittarius. Radio astronomy was born.
strumenti/jansky/origine: In his honour, the unit used to measure the strength of radio sources is called the jansky.
strumenti/jansky/curiosita: People called it "Jansky's merry-go-round", because it turned round once every twenty minutes.
strumenti/arecibo/cosa: A 305-metre dish nestled inside a natural sinkhole, with the receiving antenna hung above it on cables. For more than fifty years it was the largest single-dish radio telescope in the world.
strumenti/arecibo/dove: Near Arecibo, on the island of Puerto Rico (Caribbean).
strumenti/arecibo/quando: From 1963 until 1 December 2020, when the suspended platform collapsed after some of its cables snapped.
strumenti/arecibo/scoperte: In 1965 it measured that Mercury spins on its axis in 59 days. In 1974 the first binary pulsar was discovered there, which confirmed Einstein's relativity (Nobel Prize 1993). In 1992 the first planets outside the Solar System were found there, orbiting a pulsar.
strumenti/arecibo/origine: It takes its name from the town of Arecibo, which according to tradition is named after a Taíno chief, Arasibo.
strumenti/arecibo/curiosita: On 16 November 1974 the "Arecibo message", a picture in binary code, was beamed from Arecibo towards the globular cluster M13: it will get there in about 25,000 years. The telescope appears in the films GoldenEye and Contact.
strumenti/vlt/cosa: Four large telescopes with 8.2-metre mirrors, plus four 1.8-metre auxiliary telescopes, which can work alone or together. It is the main observatory of ESO, the European Southern Observatory, of which Italy is also a member.
strumenti/vlt/dove: On Cerro Paranal, at 2,635 metres, in the Atacama Desert in Chile: one of the driest and darkest places on Earth.
strumenti/vlt/quando: The first of the four telescopes saw first light in 1998.
strumenti/vlt/scoperte: In 2004, the first photo of a planet outside the Solar System (2M1207b). For years it followed the stars orbiting the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way: for this research Reinhard Genzel won the Nobel Prize in 2020. It also helped discover Proxima b, the planet of the nearest star to the Sun.
strumenti/vlt/origine: Very Large Telescope means just what it says: "a very large telescope". The four telescopes have names in the Mapuche language of Chile: Antu (Sun), Kueyen (Moon), Melipal (Southern Cross) and Yepun (Venus).
strumenti/vlt/curiosita: Those names were suggested in 1999 by a 17-year-old Chilean girl who won a competition. The hotel for the staff at Paranal appears in the James Bond film Quantum of Solace.
strumenti/keck/cosa: Two twin telescopes with 10-metre mirrors, each made of 36 hexagonal segments that work as a single mirror. It was the first large telescope with a "segmented" mirror, an idea that all the giants use today.
strumenti/keck/dove: On the summit of Mauna Kea, an extinct volcano in Hawaii, at 4,145 metres.
strumenti/keck/quando: Keck I in 1993, Keck II in 1996.
strumenti/keck/scoperte: Andrea Ghez used it to measure the orbits of the stars around the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way: Nobel Prize in Physics 2020. In 2008, together with the Gemini telescope, it took the first pictures of a whole system of planets around another star (HR 8799). It helped discover that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.
strumenti/keck/origine: It is named after the foundation of William Myron Keck, an oilman, which paid for its construction. Mauna Kea means "white mountain" in Hawaiian, because the summit is covered in snow in winter.
strumenti/keck/curiosita: For Native Hawaiians the summit of Mauna Kea is sacred, and building new telescopes up there has been at the centre of protests for years.
strumenti/gtc/cosa: The optical telescope with the largest single mirror in the world: 10.4 metres, made up of 36 hexagonal segments. It is Spanish, with Mexico and the University of Florida as partners.
strumenti/gtc/dove: At the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, at about 2,300 metres, on the island of La Palma (Canary Islands, Spain).
strumenti/gtc/quando: First light in 2007, scientific observations since 2009.
strumenti/gtc/scoperte: It studies extremely distant galaxies, exploding stars, black holes and the small icy bodies beyond Neptune.
strumenti/gtc/origine: Gran Telescopio Canarias, or GranTeCan to its friends. Roque de los Muchachos means "rock of the boys", after some rocks that from a distance look like the figures of young men.
strumenti/gtc/curiosita: Since 1988 the Canary Islands have had a "sky law" that limits night-time lighting to protect the observatories from light pollution.
strumenti/tng/cosa: Italy's largest optical telescope, with a 3.58-metre mirror. It is run by INAF, Italy's National Institute for Astrophysics.
strumenti/tng/dove: On the island of La Palma (Canary Islands), next to the Gran Telescopio Canarias, at about 2,400 metres.
strumenti/tng/scoperte: With its HARPS-N instrument it measures the masses of planets around other stars with great precision. In 2013 it helped show that the planet Kepler-78b has a density similar to the Earth's, which means it is made of rock and iron.
strumenti/tng/origine: Named after Galileo Galilei, the first person to point a telescope at the sky.
strumenti/tng/curiosita: It is in Spain rather than Italy because over the Alps and the Apennines the sky is too damp and too brightly lit: the Canary Islands have clear, calm air above the clouds.
strumenti/lbt/tipo: Two 8.4-metre mirrors on a single mount
strumenti/lbt/cosa: A giant pair of "binoculars": two 8.4-metre mirrors mounted side by side. Used together they collect as much light as an 11.8-metre mirror and see detail like one almost 23 metres across. Italy, through INAF, owns a quarter of it and built some of its instruments.
strumenti/lbt/dove: On Mount Graham, in Arizona (United States), at 3,221 metres.
strumenti/lbt/scoperte: Using both mirrors together it photographed the lava lakes on Jupiter's moon Io, 600 million km away. It is one of the best in the world at "adaptive optics", which corrects the shimmering of the air in real time.
strumenti/lbt/origine: Large Binocular Telescope: a big two-eyed telescope.
strumenti/lbt/curiosita: On the same mountain stands the telescope of the Vatican Observatory, the Pope's observatory.
strumenti/alma/cosa: Sixty-six dish antennas, 12 and 7 metres across, that work together as a single telescope up to 16 km wide. It sees the cold gas and dust where stars and planets are born, which are invisible to ordinary telescopes.
strumenti/alma/dove: On the Chajnantor plateau, at 5,000 metres, in the Atacama Desert in Chile.
strumenti/alma/quando: Opened in 2013. It is a partnership between Europe (ESO), North America and East Asia, together with Chile.
strumenti/alma/scoperte: In 2014 it captured for the first time the rings in a disc of dust around a young star, HL Tauri: the gaps are probably carved out by planets that are forming. It is one of the key antennas of the Event Horizon Telescope.
strumenti/alma/origine: ALMA stands for Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array; in Spanish "alma" means soul.
strumenti/alma/curiosita: The antennas, weighing 100 tonnes each, are moved around to change the layout of the array by two enormous lorries called Otto and Lore. The technicians up there breathe from oxygen bottles.
strumenti/eht/tipo: An Earth-sized network of radio telescopes
strumenti/eht/cosa: It is not a single telescope but a network of radio telescopes scattered all over the world (Chile, Hawaii, Spain, Mexico, the South Pole and elsewhere) that observe together on the same night. By combining their data using atomic clocks, they become a virtual telescope as big as the Earth.
strumenti/eht/dove: Wherever there is a suitable radio telescope: from the Andes to the South Pole.
strumenti/eht/quando: The first big campaign was in April 2017.
strumenti/eht/scoperte: On 10 April 2019 it revealed the first image of a black hole, the one at the centre of the galaxy M87, 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. On 12 May 2022 came the image of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of our own Milky Way.
strumenti/eht/origine: The event horizon is the boundary of a black hole: beyond that limit nothing, not even light, can get back out.
strumenti/eht/curiosita: There was so much data that it couldn't be sent over the Internet: it travelled by plane on hundreds of hard drives.
strumenti/srt/cosa: Italy's largest radio telescope: a 64-metre dish with an "active" surface, made of panels moved by small motors that adjust it by fractions of a millimetre to keep it perfect as the telescope tilts. It is one of INAF's three large Italian radio telescopes, together with those at Medicina and Noto (each has its own page).
strumenti/srt/dove: At San Basilio, in southern Sardinia, about 35 km from Cagliari.
strumenti/srt/scoperte: It studies pulsars, galaxies and the Sun, and works with European and worldwide networks of radio telescopes. The Italian Space Agency also uses it to communicate with probes in space.
strumenti/srt/origine: Sardinia Radio Telescope: simply the radio telescope of Sardinia.
strumenti/srt/curiosita: It was designed by the radio astronomers at Medicina, who came up with the idea in 1999: construction began in 2003.
strumenti/medicina/nome: The Medicina radio telescope and the Northern Cross
strumenti/medicina/cosa: The cradle of Italian radio astronomy. It has two instruments: the Northern Cross, a huge antenna made of long rows of metal "cylinders" laid out in a T, one of the largest radio telescopes in the world by surface area; and a 32-metre dish that can point anywhere in the sky. They are run by INAF's Institute of Radio Astronomy.
strumenti/medicina/dove: Out in the open countryside in the municipality of Medicina, about 30 km from Bologna. Next to it is the "Marcello Ceccarelli" Visitor Centre, open to the public since 2005.
strumenti/medicina/quando: Radio astronomy in Bologna began in 1959 and the first prototype was set up in 1960. The Northern Cross was opened in November 1964 and worked at full capacity from 1967; the 32-metre dish was opened in 1983.
strumenti/medicina/scoperte: The Northern Cross was used to compile the "Bologna" catalogues of radio sources: the first, in 1968, listed 328 of them, the second (B2) thousands. In July 1994 the dish picked up the signal of water vapour released when comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashed into Jupiter. On 3 March 2021 the Northern Cross recorded its first "fast radio burst" (FRB), a pulse lasting 8 thousandths of a second that came from a galaxy 485 million light years away.
strumenti/medicina/origine: The radio telescope takes its name from the town. According to tradition, Medicina (Italian for "medicine") owes its name to a potion that cured the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The Northern Cross is named after its shape (originally it really was a cross) and recalls the asterism of the same name in the constellation of Cygnus.
strumenti/medicina/curiosita: The Northern Cross was dreamt up by Marcello Ceccarelli, the physicist who founded Italian radio astronomy. Today part of the antenna, together with the Italian Space Agency, also keeps watch on space debris orbiting the Earth, and the dish takes part in networks of radio telescopes that link up antennas all over the world (VLBI).
strumenti/noto/cosa: A 32-metre dish that weighs more than 300 tonnes and turns on a circular rail. It is the twin of the one at Medicina, but it has an active surface: 240 panels pushed by 244 small motors that correct the distortions caused by its weight, so it can also observe the shortest radio waves, just a few millimetres long. It is run by INAF's Institute of Radio Astronomy.
strumenti/noto/dove: In the Renna Bassa area, in the municipality of Noto, in the province of Syracuse (Sicily). It is one of the southernmost radio telescopes in Europe, and from there it can see lower down towards the southern sky.
strumenti/noto/quando: Opened on 28 October 1988. In 2010 a bearing in one of the wheels broke: after two years out of action and about a million euros' worth of work, it was back observing in January 2012.
strumenti/noto/scoperte: It works mainly in networks with antennas all over the world (VLBI) to study quasars, galaxy cores and newborn stars in great detail. It is also used for geodesy: by precisely measuring the distances between antennas very far apart, scientists can see how many millimetres a year the continents move, including Sicily being pushed by Africa. It is also used to track space probes and debris in orbit.
strumenti/noto/origine: It takes its name from the town of Noto, the ancient Roman Netum, famous for its Baroque architecture, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
strumenti/noto/curiosita: Since 2012 it has been connected by optical fibre to the Italian research network: its data reach the European centre that combines them with those from the other antennas in real time (e-VLBI), without having to ship hard drives.
strumenti/fast/cosa: The largest single-dish radio telescope in the world: 500 metres across, the area of about thirty football pitches, built in a natural hollow among the hills.
strumenti/fast/dove: In Guizhou province, in southern China.
strumenti/fast/scoperte: It has discovered more than a thousand pulsars, dead stars that spin incredibly fast and send out regular radio pulses like a lighthouse.
strumenti/fast/origine: FAST stands for Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope. In Chinese it is called Tianyan, "Eye of Heaven".
strumenti/fast/curiosita: Around the telescope there is a radio-quiet zone 5 km wide: some villages were moved to build it, and visitors are asked to leave their phones behind.
